articles.title: Bill Gates says to prepare for 20 years of ‘tumultuous’ AI disruption
articles.summary: Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation. You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late August titled “The turbulent AI era is
body: The Microsoft cofounder isn’t an AI doomer, but he says it’s still “the most dangerous weapon of all time.”

In his piece, Gates ratcheted up his rhetoric around AI safety, writing that “even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history.”

In interviews since, Gates has called AI “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near,” and that AI “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing.” It is clear he does not think the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated efforts from the AI industry itself, is sufficient to combat this threat.

So I wanted to know: Is Bill Gates an AI doomer? I also had a series of questions downstream from what he’s been arguing about AI. How can we ever hope to control AI, and align it to humanity, if we can’t even agree on what it is and whether it’s conscious? How would you even technically construct a solution to alignment that could be enforced, not just for closed-source models but open-source ones, too?

articles.title: Eiliko maker says it’s hiring an ‘independent security firm’ after Verge report on its insecure robots
articles.summary: Eiliko, a cute robot charm you can hang on your bag with built-in AI conversations, turned out to be a security nightmare. It told owners that "your secrets are safe with me," but hackers could easily read complete transcripts of everything we told the toy, and that was just the beginning.
body: Now, the company is finally breaking its silence, though its response leaves something to be desired.

“We have confirmed the core issues identified in your reporting and are addressing each of them,” Energize Lab told The Verge in an unsigned statement from a generic email address, which it later told us is attributable to CTO Du Xiaoyu. The company says it will hire an independent security firm to fully review all of its systems, and has set up a dedicated security@energizelab.com contact email.
The company also claims that as of Wednesday, it has “closed all external access to our backend systems” and “disabled the interface that allowed a robot’s responses to be modified remotely.”

Energize Labs is also pledging to “no longer store conversation records or the user profiles generated from them,” and says it will delete the conversation records, user profiles, and “avatar images” it has already stored.

articles.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
articles.summary: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds?
body: Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.
points: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon.
But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.
Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

articles.title: 1Password lets AI agents use your passwords without seeing them
articles.summary: 1Password is introducing a new feature that allows AI agents to sign into your accounts without actually seeing or handling your passwords. The aptly named 1Password for Agents doesn't give bots free reign to access all of your connected accounts - you'll still need to grant approval for sign-in…
body: Just grant the agent access approval and it’ll sign into your accounts to complete tasks.

”Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf. The old model where you hand over a credential and hope for the best doesn’t work,” 1Password chief product officer Aashish Tripathi said in a press statement. “An agent should be able to do the job it’s been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences.”

With this new system, an AI agent uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password when it reaches a sign-in form. The app then sends you a notification about which account credentials it needs, and why. If you choose to approve the request, 1Password will fill in the required login information instead of handing it to the agent. Approvals are granted on your own device to ensure you’re behind the permissions, making this a similar process to two-factor authentication. After the agent is signed in, it’ll continue with its task, without ever having actually seen your password.

articles.title: AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary.
articles.summary: Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience. Tech companies have marketed them as personal assistants - the democratizing of labor that ordinarily would only be available to the rich and powerful.
body: AI agents are getting blocked left and right — but even when they work, it suggests a more annoying future for humans.

Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have all introduced some version of agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is. Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf. But as AI companies — and their users — are finding out, buying things requires that the other party is willing to sell them in the first place.

Even without hard blocks, agents’ access to retailers is spotty. For example, Muse, which I instructed to look for a specific face moisturizer, was caught in Target’s bot check one day but was able to get through the next. It suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to my address when I searched for the best price on granola bars. When I asked for mattress recommendations under a certain price point, Muse was once again blocked by Target, despite being able to pull from the site just a few minutes prior.
points: Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience.

articles.title: Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
articles.summary: A global map categorizing every 10-meter patch of land on Earth into distinct forest types.
body: Protecting the planet's forests starts with a simple question: what type of forest are we looking at? From space, an old-growth rainforest, a eucalyptus plantation, and an oil palm estate can look like the same patch of green. But they hold very different amounts of carbon and biodiversity. Telling them apart, and knowing how each patch has changed over time, shows us where conservation is working and where natural forests are being converted into plantations and farms.

All forests store carbon and, together, forests are home to most of the world's land-based plant and animal species. But a forest’s ecological value also depends on its history: a primary forest that has never been cleared holds far more carbon and biodiversity than a single-species timber plantation that is harvested every decade or two.

articles.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
articles.summary: The new open-source model speaks the language of DNA and can help researchers understand the effects of any changes on gene activity and health.
body: The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.

Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.

Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.

“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”

articles.title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
articles.summary: Step one in convincing people to live with robots with cameras on their faces? Disguise them as cute home decor.
body: You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.

As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.

That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.

articles.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
articles.summary: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one.
body: For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

articles.title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
articles.summary: Amazon Web Services logged attempts to leverage the internet-melting PHP2Shell bugs four days ago. They’re now being “broadly exploited” across the internet.
body: The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
articles.summary: Meta’s board feared that its CEO’s departure could disrupt the company’s AI ambitions. A new stock agreement gives him financial incentives to stay put.
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

articles.title: What FDE means at OpenAI
articles.summary: What forward deployed engineering means at OpenAI
body: When Codex came out, someone on the team asked me, “What do we do when Codex can just one-shot the use cases we spent the last few months building?”

That question gets to the heart of what FDE means at OpenAI. We work alongside customers to understand their hardest problems and build solutions they can depend on. What we learn helps shape our products and gives Research concrete problems to solve.
That is progress. If we make ourselves obsolete every couple of months, our FDE team is doing its job.
I founded the team in early 2025 to close what we call “the deployment gap”: the distance between what models appear capable of and what people can reliably use to do their work.
